messages.subject: Power Analysis sample size
parts:
Hi All,

 

I have some combined survey data (photographic and distance sampling) that I want to run a power analysis on, to examine what change in abundance we can detect given the current abundance and precision.  I’m using a single abundance estimate to run the power analysis, assuming repeated surveys will have the same level of precision. The R function I’d like to use requires a sample size (function tTestLnormAltPower from the EnvStats package).  

 

Can I use the df computed from Satterthwaite’s (1946) method, for the combined survey data as an approximation of the sample size?  Or can someone recommend an alternative approach for approximating sample size or an alternative type of power analysis that doesn’t rely on sample size?

 

Thanks,

Mitch

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Power Analysis sample size
parts:
Hello again Mitch

Chapter 5 of the Advanced Distance Sampling text (Buckland et al. 2004) is entitled "Temporal inferences from distance sampling surveys".  That chapter discusses means of assessing power to detect change from a series of surveys.  The computations described therein are not dependent upon sample size determination, but rather upon precision in the resulting density or abundance estimates.

There is companion R code used to create some of the figures in the chapter to be found here at Len Thomas' web site:
http://lenthomas.org/software/rtrend.zip

parts:
Mitch

You are right to scratch your head when performing the calculations in Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).  Because with a pooled detection function there are parameters of only a single detection function to estimate rather than two sets of parameters.  That can result in some reduction in uncertainty, but in most line transect survey situations that reduction is modest, because the greatest proportion of uncertainty in density estimates derive from variability in encounter rates between transects.

Use of the Sattherthwaite correction makes a difference in the calculations when there are a small number of transects.  Hopefully, if you are in the design stage, you can design to have a sufficient number of replicate transects.

Thanks,

Mitch

parts:
Hi Mitch,

I'm maybe (very plausibly!) misunderstanding something about the analyses you're describing, but the numbers you quote for the Power Analysis don't seem right. A CV of 5% for a population estimate sounds tight. A decline in abundance of 50% p.a. is catastrophic. Starting from a relative abundance index of 1, 5 years of decline of this scale takes you to a year 5 index of 0.03. The notion that you could estimate population size to within 5% but not have the power to detect population decline until you were at 3% of your initial level seems wrong. I don't think actual abundances matter very much (the effect of actual abundance on your power to detect declines will be through encounter rates, which will be a product of detectability and abundance. But this should, I think, be wrapped up in your CV of 5%.

Apologies if I've misunderstood anything here. But it seems to me like the power analysis is off-kilter here. Eric or others on the list may have more erudite views.

Best wishes,

Mark

Mitch, bear in mind that this is based on a t-test with just 3df for 5 years of data, and 2 df for 4 years of data.  So you are testing whether a slope differs significantly from zero on the basis of just 4 or 5 points, and for this analysis you estimate the cv from a very small sample size.  If you assumed the cv were known, or used the annual estimates of cv in your analysis, you would get very different answers.  The power calculation just estimates the cv from the departures of the estimates from a fitted line.  This is fine for a reasonably long time series of estimates, but probably not a good strategy for very short sequences.

 

Steve

The 2001 distance sampling book gives an example of a pairwise comparison.  This approach could be extended to more than 2 estimates.  E.g. if you have 3 estimates E1, E2 and E3, you could take -1.E1 + 0.E2 + 1.E3, find its variance, and hence test whether the value differs significantly from zero.  To test for curvature in the trend, you could take -1.E1 + 2.E2 -1.E3, again finds its variance, then test whether it differs significantly from zero.

 

There are no doubt other solutions!

Steve

On Friday, 24 April 2020 09:05:20 UTC-7, Stephen Buckland wrote:

Mitch, bear in mind that this is based on a t-test with just 3df for 5 years of data, and 2 df for 4 years of data.  So you are testing whether a slope differs significantly from zero on the basis of just 4 or 5 points, and for this analysis you estimate the cv from a very small sample size.  If you assumed the cv were known, or used the annual estimates of cv in your analysis, you would get very different answers.  The power calculation just estimates the cv from the departures of the estimates from a fitted line.  This is fine for a reasonably long time series of estimates, but probably not a good strategy for very short sequences.

 

Steve

I'm maybe (very plausibly!) misunderstanding something about the analyses you're describing, but the numbers you quote for the Power Analysis don't seem right. A CV of 5% for a population estimate sounds tight. A decline in abundance of 50% p.a. is catastrophic. Starting from a relative abundance index of 1, 5 years of decline of this scale takes you to a year 5 index of 0.03. Best wishes,

 

Mark

On Wednesday, 15 April 2020 09:41:29 UTC-7, Eric Rexstad wrote:

Mitch

 

You are right to scratch your head when performing the calculations in Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).  Because with a pooled detection function there are parameters of only a single detection function to estimate rather than two sets of parameters.  That can result in some reduction in uncertainty, but in most line transect survey situations that reduction is modest, because the greatest proportion of uncertainty in density estimates derive from variability in encounter rates between transects.

 

Use of the Sattherthwaite correction makes a difference in the calculations when there are a small number of transects.  Hopefully, if you are in the design stage, you can design to have a sufficient number of replicate transects.

On Tuesday, 28 April 2020 02:12:08 UTC-7, Stephen Buckland wrote:

The 2001 distance sampling book gives an example of a pairwise comparison.  This approach could be extended to more than 2 estimates.  E.g. if you have 3 estimates E1, E2 and E3, you could take -1.E1 + 0.E2 + 1.E3, find its variance, and hence test whether the value differs significantly from zero.  To test for curvature in the trend, you could take -1.E1 + 2.E2 -1.E3, again finds its variance, then test whether it differs significantly from zero.

 

There are no doubt other solutions!

Mitch, bear in mind that this is based on a t-test with just 3df for 5 years of data, and 2 df for 4 years of data.  So you are testing whether a slope differs significantly from zero on the basis of just 4 or 5 points, and for this analysis you estimate the cv from a very small sample size.  If you assumed the cv were known, or used the annual estimates of cv in your analysis, you would get very different answers.  The power calculation just estimates the cv from the departures of the estimates from a fitted line.  This is fine for a reasonably long time series of estimates, but probably not a good strategy for very short sequences.

I'm maybe (very plausibly!) misunderstanding something about the analyses you're describing, but the numbers you quote for the Power Analysis don't seem right. A CV of 5% for a population estimate sounds tight. A decline in abundance of 50% p.a. is catastrophic. On Wednesday, 15 April 2020 09:41:29 UTC-7, Eric Rexstad wrote:

Mitch

 

You are right to scratch your head when performing the calculations in Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).  Because with a pooled detection function there are parameters of only a single detection function to estimate rather than two sets of parameters.  That can result in some reduction in uncertainty, but in most line transect survey situations that reduction is modest, because the greatest proportion of uncertainty in density estimates derive from variability in encounter rates between transects.

 

Use of the Sattherthwaite correction makes a difference in the calculations when there are a small number of transects.  Hopefully, if you are in the design stage, you can design to have a sufficient number of replicate transects.

Chapter 5 of the Advanced Distance Sampling text (Buckland et al. 2004) is entitled "Temporal inferences from distance sampling surveys".  That chapter discusses means of assessing power to detect change from a series of surveys.  The computations described therein are not dependent upon sample size determination, but rather upon precision in the resulting density or abundance estimates.
